title: Physics and Measurement
notes:
What is Physics?

Physics is the branch of science that studies natural phenomena — from subatomic particles (10⁻¹⁵ m) to the entire observable universe (10²⁶ m). The word derives from the Greek physika (\phi\sigma\iota\kappa\alpha), meaning "things natural." In Sanskrit, it is called Bhautika (भूतिक), referring to the physical world. Physics investigates matter, energy, space, time, and their interactions. Its fundamental aim is to discover the laws of nature — simple mathematical principles that govern all physical phenomena.

Branches of Mechanics

Mechanics is the oldest branch of physics, dealing with bodies at rest or in motion. It is divided into: Statics — study of bodies in equilibrium (at rest or moving with constant velocity); Kinematics — description of motion WITHOUT reference to its causes (derived from Greek kinema, meaning "motion"); Dynamics — study of motion AND its causes (forces, mass); derived from Greek dynamis (power). Kinematics answers "how does it move?" Dynamics answers "why does it move?"

Fundamental vs. Derived Quantities

Fundamental (base) quantities are independent — they cannot be defined in terms of other quantities. There are seven SI fundamental quantities: Length [L], Mass [M], Time [T], Electric current [I], Temperature [K], Amount of substance [N], Luminous intensity [J]. Derived quantities are defined using fundamental quantities through mathematical relationships. Examples: Area = length × breadth → [L²]; Speed = displacement/time → [LT⁻¹]; Force = mass × acceleration → [MLT⁻²]; Energy = force × distance → [ML²T⁻²].

Physical Quantities: Definition and Expression

A physical quantity is any property of nature that can be measured. Every physical quantity is expressed as: Quantity = Numerical value (n) \times Unit (u). For example, length l = 5 m means the numerical value is 5 and the unit is meter. If the same length is expressed in cm: l = 500 cm. The numerical value changes (5 → 500) but the physical quantity remains the same. This gives the principle of unit conversion: n₁u₁ = n₂u₂, so n₂ = n₁(u₁/u₂).

S.I. Units — The International System

The Système International d'Unités (SI) was established in 1960 by the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM). It provides a coherent system where all derived units are expressed in terms of the seven base units without numerical conversion factors. Base units: meter (m) for length, kilogram (kg) for mass, second (s) for time, ampere (A) for current, kelvin (K) for temperature, mole (mol) for amount, candela (cd) for luminous intensity. Supplementary units (radian rad for plane angle, steradian sr for solid angle) are dimensionless derived units used for convenience.

Units of Length

Length measurement spans an enormous range in physics: Subatomic: Fermi (fm) = 10⁻¹⁵ m (nuclear size). Atomic: Angstrom (\AA) = 10⁻¹⁰ m (atomic radius). Macroscopic: Meter (m) = standard unit. Astronomical: Astronomical Unit (AU) = 1.5 \times 10¹¹ m (Earth-Sun distance). Light year (ly) = 9.46 \times 10¹⁵ m (distance light travels in one year). Parsec (pc) = 3.26 ly = 3.08 \times 10¹⁶ m (used for stellar distances; 1 pc is the distance at which 1 AU subtends 1 arcsecond).

Units of Mass

The kilogram (kg) is the SI unit of mass. Historically defined by a platinum-iridium cylinder kept at Sèvres, France. Since May 20, 2019, the kilogram is defined by fixing the numerical value of Planck's constant h = 6.62607015 \times 10⁻³⁴ J·s. Other mass units: gram (g) = 10⁻³ kg; atomic mass unit (u or amu) = 1.66053906660 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (defined as 1/12 the mass of a carbon-12 atom); tonne (t) = 1000 kg. Mass is a measure of inertia — the resistance of a body to change in its state of motion.

Units of Time

The second (s) is the SI unit of time. Originally defined as 1/86400 of a mean solar day. Since 1967, it is defined by the cesium-133 atom: the duration of 9,192,631,770 periods of the radiation corresponding to the transition between two hyperfine levels of the ground state. Atomic clocks based on this definition are accurate to within 1 second in 100 million years. Other units: minute (min) = 60 s; hour (h) = 3600 s; day = 86400 s; year = 365.25 days ≈ 3.156 \times 10⁷ s.

Dimensions and Dimensional Formula

The dimensions of a physical quantity are the powers to which the fundamental quantities (M, L, T, etc.) must be raised to represent that quantity. For example: Force = mass \times acceleration → [Force] = [M] \times [LT⁻²] = [MLT⁻²]. This is called the dimensional formula. A dimensional equation equates a quantity to its formula: [F] = [MLT⁻²]. Dimensions provide a shorthand for understanding the structure of physical laws and checking equations. The concept was systematically introduced by Joseph Fourier in 1822.

Dimensional Analysis and Its Power

Dimensional analysis uses the principle of homogeneity (dimensions on both sides must match) to: (1) Check correctness of equations, (2) Derive relationships between quantities, (3) Convert between unit systems. It CANNOT: determine dimensionless constants, handle trigonometric/exponential functions directly, or work with more than 3 unknown exponents. The method assumes a power-law relationship and solves for exponents by equating dimensions. This technique is used in fluid dynamics (Reynolds number), aerodynamics (drag coefficients), and all areas of physics where relationships between variables are being explored.
confusion: Mass and weight are NOT the same — Mass (kg) is the amount of matter and a measure of inertia; it is scalar and constant everywhere. Weight (N) is the gravitational force on a mass: W = mg; it is a vector and varies with location (different on Earth vs. Moon).

Mole and mol are NOT the same thing — Mole (with capital M) sometimes denotes molar mass (kg/mol); mol (lowercase) is the SI unit symbol for amount of substance. One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 \times 10²³ elementary entities (Avogadro's number).

Plane angle and solid angle are dimensionless but carry special units — Radian (rad) and steradian (sr) are derived units that are equivalent to [M⁰L⁰T⁰]. They are treated as 'supplementary' rather than 'fundamental' in SI. Don't include them in dimensional equations.

The unit of a quantity can change but its dimensions cannot — Force always has dimensions [MLT⁻²] whether measured in Newton (SI) or dyne (CGS) or pound-force. Changing units changes the numerical value (n₁u₁ = n₂u₂), not the dimensions.

Fundamental quantities are chosen by CONVENTION, not necessity — We choose M, L, T as base because they are independent in mechanics. But we COULD choose F, L, T instead (then M = FL⁻¹T²). The resulting dimensional formulas change form but physical laws remain identical.

Dimensionless constants like \pi and e appear in physical formulas but are NOT dimensions — In T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}, the 2\pi is a pure number with no dimensions. Dimensional analysis cannot predict it; only experiment or deeper theory can.

Significant figures indicate precision, NOT accuracy — Reporting 3.00 cm means you measured to \pm 0.01 cm precision, but the true value could be 3.05 cm (accurate?) — accuracy depends on calibration, significant figures depend on the instrument's resolution.

Light year is a UNIT OF DISTANCE, not time — Despite containing 'year,' a light year = 9.46 \times 10¹⁵ meters. It measures how far light travels in one year. Parsec (3.26 light years) is even larger and is the standard unit in professional astronomy.
practice: Convert 1 Newton to dyne using dimensional analysis. [Solution: [F] = [MLT⁻²]. 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². In CGS: 1 N = 1 \times (1000 g)(100 cm)/s² = 10⁵ g·cm/s² = 10⁵ dyne.]
The density of a material is 2.7 g/cm³. Convert to kg/m³. [Solution: 2.7 g/cm³ \times (1 kg/1000 g)(100 cm/1 m)³ = 2.7 \times 10⁻³ \times 10⁶ = 2700 kg/m³.]
If the unit of length is 10 m, unit of mass is 10 kg, and unit of time is 1 s, find the unit of force in this system. [Solution: [F] = [MLT⁻²] = (10 kg)(10 m)(1 s)⁻² = 100 kg·m/s² = 100 newtons.]

Express the speed of light (3 \times 10⁸ m/s) in km/year. [Solution: 3 \times 10⁸ m/s \times (1 km/1000 m) \times (3600 s/h)(24 h/day)(365.25 day/year) = 3 \times 10⁵ \times 3.15576 \times 10⁷ = 9.467 \times 10¹² km/year.]

Check the dimensional correctness of the equation: v² = u² + 2as. [Solution: LHS: [v²] = [LT⁻¹]² = [L²T⁻²]. RHS term 1: [u²] = [L²T⁻²]. RHS term 2: [2as] = [LT⁻²][L] = [L²T⁻²]. All terms have [L²T⁻²]. The equation is dimensionally correct.]

A light year is the distance light travels in one year. Calculate it in meters. (c = 3 \times 10⁸ m/s, 1 year = 365.25 days.) [Solution: 1 ly = (3 \times 10⁸ m/s)(365.25 \times 24 \times 3600 s) = 3 \times 10⁸ \times 3.15576 \times 10⁷ = 9.467 \times 10¹⁵ m \approx 9.46 \times 10¹⁵ m.]

The viscosity of water at 20°C is 1.002 mPa\cdot s. Convert to Poise (CGS unit). [Solution: 1 mPa\cdot s = 10⁻³ Pa\cdot s = 10⁻³ (N\cdot s/m²) = 10⁻³ (kg/m\cdot s). In CGS: 10⁻³ \times (1000 g/kg)(100 cm/m)⁻¹ = 10⁻³ \times 10 = 10⁻² Poise = 0.01 Poise. So 1.002 mPa\cdot s = 0.01002 Poise.]

Show that the dimensional formula of Planck's constant h is [ML²T⁻¹] and explain its significance. [Solution: From E = h\nu, [h] = [E]/[\nu] = [ML²T⁻²]/[T⁻¹] = [ML²T⁻¹]. This equals the dimensions of angular momentum [mvr] = [M][LT⁻¹][L] = [ML²T⁻¹]. Significance: h is the quantum of action and sets the scale of quantum effects; it appears in the uncertainty principle \Delta x \cdot \Delta p \geq \hbar/2.]

The kinetic energy KE = \frac{1}{2}mv². If mass is measured with 2% error and velocity with 3% error, find the percentage error in KE. [Solution: \frac{\Delta KE}{KE} = \frac{\Delta m}{m} + 2\frac{\Delta v}{v} = 2\% + 2(3\%) = 2\% + 6\% = 8\%.]

Using dimensional analysis, derive the formula for the period T of a simple pendulum in terms of length l, mass m, and acceleration due to gravity g. State whether mass affects the period. [Solution: Assume T = kl^a m^b g^c. [T] = [L]^a [M]^b [LT⁻²]^c = [M^b L^{a+c} T^{-2c}]. Equating: b = 0 (mass doesn't affect period!), a + c = 0, -2c = 1 \Rightarrow c = -½, a = ½. T = k\sqrt{l/g}. Mass m drops out — period is independent of mass, depending only on l and g.]
universalFacts: The meter was originally defined as 1/10,000,000 of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator (1793) — Today it is defined by the speed of light: 1 m = distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 second. This makes the meter universal and reproducible anywhere with the right equipment.

NEB exam tip: When asked about the smallest/largest practical units of length, remember: Fermi (10⁻¹⁵ m) for nuclear physics and Parsec (3.08 \times 10¹⁶ m) for astronomy. Light year is larger but Parsec is the professional astronomy standard because it arises naturally from parallax measurements.

The seven SI base units were redefined in 2019 using fundamental constants — kilogram via Planck's constant h, ampere via elementary charge e, kelvin via Boltzmann constant k_B, mole via Avogadro constant N_A. This ended the era of artifact-based definitions (the international prototype kilogram kept in Paris).

Ancient Indian texts like the Rig Veda and Atharva Veda describe concepts of time (kshana = 49 ms) and length (paramanu ≈ atomic scale) — These early attempts at quantification show that the need for standardized measurement predates modern science by millennia.

The concept of 'dimension' in physics is deeply connected to 'symmetry' in modern theory — Noether's theorem (1915) shows that conservation of energy arises from time-translation symmetry, conservation of momentum from space-translation symmetry. Dimensions are the fingerprints of these symmetries.

In Nepal, the Bureau of Standards has adopted SI units as the legal standard — Measurements for trade, education, and industry use SI. However, traditional units like 'anna' (weight), 'dhur' (area), and 'ghantas' (time) are still used in daily life. Understanding SI conversion is essential for NEB students.

The dimensionless fine-structure constant \alpha = e²/(4\pi\epsilon_0 \hbar c) \approx 1/137 is one of physics' most famous numbers — It has no units, no dimensions, yet it governs the strength of electromagnetic interactions. Its value cannot be derived from theory; it must be measured. What would the universe be like if \alpha were slightly different?
